nameStory: The grass-leaved arrowhead gets its name from its narrow, grass-like leaves that look nothing like the classic arrow shape you'd expect from an arrowhead plant. While most of its cousins sport bold, pointed leaves that clearly resemble arrowheads, this species decided to go incognito with slender foliage that could fool you into thinking it's just another piece of pond grass.
description: Grass-leaved arrowhead is an aquatic plant that grows in shallow water and muddy shores throughout eastern North America. Unlike other arrowheads with their distinctive arrow-shaped leaves, this species produces narrow, grass-like foliage that emerges from the water or sprawls along wet ground. The plant produces small white flowers on tall stalks above the water surface during summer. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall, forming colonies in suitable wetland habitats.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow leaves that look remarkably like grass blades, completely lacking the arrow shape of other arrowheads. Feel smooth and somewhat thick with parallel veins running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with three rounded petals arranged in clusters on tall, leafless stalks. Each flower about half an inch across with a bright yellow center of stamens.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Emerges from shallow water or muddy shores, often forming patches. Leaves may float on water surface or stand upright above it, connected by underground runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dense, round clusters of small, flattened seeds that feel papery and have a distinctive beak-like projection. Clusters turn brown as they mature in late summer.

habitat: Look for grass-leaved arrowhead in shallow water along pond edges, slow streams, marshes, and muddy shorelines throughout New England. It prefers still or slow-moving water less than two feet deep, often growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and other wetland plants. You'll find it in both natural wetlands and human-made ponds from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: New grass-like leaves begin emerging from underwater rhizomes in late spring, initially soft and bright green. Plants are still mostly vegetative and easily overlooked among other emerging wetland grasses.
seasonality.summer: White flowers bloom on tall stalks from June through August, making identification much easier. This is the best time to spot and identify this species when flowers are visible above the foliage.
seasonality.fall: Seed clusters mature and turn brown while leaves begin to yellow. Seeds may persist into early fall before dispersing, and leaves start dying back to the underground rhizomes.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground parts, leaving no visible trace above ground or water surface. Only the persistent rhizome system survives beneath the mud until spring.

funFact: This plant is like a master of disguise in the plant world – it's the only arrowhead species that completely abandoned the arrow-shaped leaves that give the whole family its name, choosing instead to blend in perfectly with ordinary pond grasses until it blooms and reveals its true identity!
confusionNotes: Before flowering, grass-leaved arrowhead looks almost identical to various wetland grasses and sedges. The key difference is the flowers – true grasses have tiny, inconspicuous flowers without petals, while this arrowhead produces showy white, three-petaled flowers on separate stalks. Memory trick: 'Grass fakes it till it makes it' – wait for the obvious flowers to confirm it's not actually grass.
contextualKnowledge: Many people expect all arrowhead plants to have arrow-shaped leaves, so this species often surprises botanists and nature enthusiasts. The scientific name 'graminea' literally means 'grass-like,' acknowledging this unusual departure from the typical family appearance. It's a perfect example of how common names can sometimes be misleading in plant identification.
compareHints: Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves. Broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and much larger flowers, while slender arrowhead has thin leaves but they're still arrow-shaped rather than grass-like. The leaf shape alone separates this species from all its relatives in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
